name: Maya Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, out by seven. First call's Mr Doyle, he had a stroke, so it's the hoist, a wash, breakfast and his tablets. Then three more before lunch, a gap, and the teatime and bedtime calls. I've done it seven years for Brightwater Home Care, and I know every key safe on the route.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars, like Mrs Kaur, who tells me the same story about her wedding and I still laugh. What wears me out is the driving and the short calls. The weekends pay time and a half, so I do most of them, which is why I'm on better money than most. My partner Tom and I have about nine months of wages put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most things that get announced. Big noise, then you still have to get Mr Doyle out of bed at half seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots never turned up to do the hoist, but quietly, because I don't like a row in the office. Online I don't post much, so I'd say nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, because I like my job the way it is. Seven years in, I know every client's front door and which ones need the key safe code said twice. If the only change is the office getting quicker at the rota, that suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my rounds and keep doing the weekend shifts, because that's where the extra money is. Tom and I put about 400 a month into savings and I'd carry on with that. Maybe in a year we'd look at a deposit for a small house near the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored of hearing about it, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the office getting quicker at the rota. Would that touch your day at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe they'd send my visits to the phone instead of the paper sheet, which I'd moan about for a week. My manager Lorraine already tried that once and half of us kept printing it out anyway. As long as the visit times stay the same length, I don't really care how they're planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the job that would still be there in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rushing. Fifteen-minute calls for someone who needs forty, that's what wears me down, not computers. Mrs Kaur gets upset if I'm in and out, and in a world where nothing changes, nothing fixes that either.

say: I'd say quietly that the **robots never turned up** to do the hoisting.
I'd keep it **off social media**, because I don't post much and don't like arguments.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because I like the job exactly as it is after seven years.
If AI only speeds up the **office rota**, that suits me fine.
do: Keep the **weekend shifts**, because that's where the extra pay comes from.
Keep putting about **400 a month** into savings with my partner Tom.
Look at a **house deposit** near the ring road within a year.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored of hearing about AI.
S0.quote: Fifteen-minute calls for someone who needs forty, that's what wears me down, not computers.
fieldNote: She treats AI as **office noise**; her real complaint is short visits, not technology.
Savings and a partner's wage make her **secure**, and she knows it.
Her resistance shows in treating the **phone rota** as something to work around.

steps.text: Keep doing the weekend shifts on the agency rota
Put 400 a month into the joint savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the office and the call centres get it, and we get it later. That's how I'd read it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say care work is the safe end of the AI changes, because nobody's coding a bed bath. At work I'd back Lorraine up if she said the rota software is coming. With friends who work in offices, I'd keep my mouth shut, because some of them would be worried for real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the bits I hate, like the visit notes and the medication charts, would go onto some app with a voice thing. I'd hate learning that. But I'd still be the one with the gloves on, so my wage is probably fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my rounds and not chase anything new until I have to. If the agency made us use a voice app for notes, I'd ask one of the younger carers, Precious, to show me once. Money-wise I'd keep saving like normal and see what happens with the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me so much as for Tom's sister, who does bookings for a travel firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Precious to show you once. What happens if the agency makes the app compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, grumbling. I'm not leaving a job I like over a phone app, there's plenty of agencies but they'd all be the same. I'd just be slow at it for a month, and I'd write it on paper first and copy it in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life feels this picture first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's sister Jade, for sure. She books coach holidays for a living, which is exactly the stuff on that card. Tom and I have talked about her moving in with us for a bit if she gets cut, and I'd be fine with that.

say: I'd say care work is the **safe end** because nobody's coding a bed bath.
I'd **stay quiet** with office friends who'd be worried for real.
think: The **visit notes** and medication charts will probably move onto an app I'd hate learning.
I'd still be the one wearing gloves, so my **wage is probably fine**.
do: Keep my **rounds** as they are and not chase anything new until forced.
Ask my colleague Precious to show me any **notes app** once.
Keep **saving as normal** and watch what happens with robots.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for her partner's sister Jade than for herself.
S1.quote: I'd say care work is the safe end of the AI changes, because nobody's coding a bed bath.
fieldNote: Her worry is aimed at **family members** in office jobs, not at her own role.
She'd adopt new tech only when **forced**, and plans to write notes on paper first.
Plenty of local agencies means she sees **no reason to move**, even if she dislikes changes.

steps.text: Keep the same morning and evening rounds without chasing anything new
Wait for the agency to bring in a notes app before learning it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's next Christmas but one. And the robots three years after, so 2031, I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what everyone would say: families won't let a machine wash their mum. I'd probably believe it on a good day. Online I'd share the odd post about keeping care human, but I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency would be first in the queue for robots, because staff are the expensive bit and we keep leaving. If a robot can do a hoist transfer and a wash for less than my hourly rate, my agency won't think twice. So I'd have about five years before my work starts to go, and I'm not the sort to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plan for now, because I wouldn't sign a mortgage on a wage that might not be there in 2031. I'd push the savings up, maybe 600 a month, by doing more weekend shifts while they're still going. Beyond that I honestly don't know, I'd wait and watch what the agency does in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knotted up. I'd be fine at work in front of clients, and then sit in the car between calls feeling sick about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on, so robots come about 3 years after the thinking AI. What does that gap mean for you, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the paperwork goes, the rota, the medication checks on the app, probably the phone calls to the GP. I'd still be going in the door every day, just with less to write. Those three years would feel like a waiting room, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and watch. With savings and three years of breathing space, why not move first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know what I'd move to, and I'm not good with new things. Tom says I should look at nursing, but that's years of study and the robots would come for that too. I'd rather hold tight with a full savings pot than jump into something I'd hate.

say: I'd say **families won't let** a machine wash their mum.
I'd share the odd post about **keeping care human**, without shouting.
think: The agency would buy **robots first**, because staff cost the most and keep leaving.
I'd have about **five years** before my work starts going, and I wouldn't be ready.
do: Put the **house purchase** on hold rather than sign a mortgage.
Raise savings to about **600 a month** with extra weekend shifts.
Watch what the agency does in the **first year** before making moves.
feel: **Knotted up**, steady with clients but sick about it in the car between calls.
S2.quote: If a robot can do a hoist transfer and a wash for less than my hourly rate, my agency won't think twice.
fieldNote: She sees the **2028 to 2031 gap** as a waiting room, not a chance to retrain.
Her **savings** buy her time, but her resistance means she'd use it to hold still.
She dismisses **nursing** because it's long study and might be automated too.

steps.text: Put the house deposit plan on hold until 2031 is clearer
Raise savings to 600 a month with extra weekend shifts
Watch what the agency buys in the first year before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking stuff, so 2031, and the robots around 2034. I'd be thirty-five then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same as the fast one, just later, and people would nod. At work we'd moan about the agency buying gadgets. I'd tell my mum not to panic, because she'd ring me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it buys me a mortgage. With eight years before a robot could do my rounds, Tom and I could buy something small and pay a big chunk off. But I still think I'd be out of this job by my late thirties, and that sits in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a smaller place than we planned, a two-bed terrace instead of a semi, and overpay it hard. I'd keep my rounds and the weekend shifts as long as they're there. Around 2031, when the notes and rota go to AI, I'd start asking Lorraine what jobs the agency keeps for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but less sick about it. Five years feels like a long countdown rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with the fast version, actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes the house, mostly. In the fast one I wouldn't sign anything, but with robots not due till 2034, my partner and I can pay a lot off the house before then. The job worry is the same, it just arrives when I'm a bit older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Lorraine, specifically, when 2031 comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they'll need someone to check on clients when the machines are in, like a person who pops round and makes sure it's all right. I'd want my name down for that early. I wouldn't want to retrain into something new, I'd want to stay near the same front doors.

say: I'd say it's the **same** as the fast one, only later.
I'd tell my mum **not to panic**, because she'd ring me about it.
think: The extra time **buys me a mortgage** I could pay a big chunk off.
I'd still expect to be **out of this job** by my late thirties.
do: Buy a **two-bed terrace** instead of a semi and overpay it.
Keep the **rounds and weekend shifts** for as long as they last.
Ask my manager in **2031** which jobs the agency keeps for people.
feel: **Worried**, but it feels like a long countdown rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a long countdown rather than a cliff.
fieldNote: The extra years change her **housing decision**, not her view of the job.
She'd want a **checking role** near the same clients rather than retraining.
Her calm with her mum hides a **private fear** about her late thirties.

steps.text: Buy a two-bed terrace instead of the semi we wanted
Overpay the mortgage hard before robots arrive around 2034
Keep the rounds and weekend shifts as long as they last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. So 2036, and the robots in 2039. I'd be forty by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and there's no point losing sleep. At work, the older carers would say they'll be retired by then, lucky them. I'd say the same thing I always say, people want people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, ten years feels like someone else's problem, and I know that's a bit daft. My job would be safe through my thirties, and that's the part of life I'm planning. By forty, who knows, maybe I'd be ready to stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the semi we wanted and probably start trying for a baby in a couple of years, like we planned. I'd keep the weekend shifts and put a bit extra into my pension. I wouldn't retrain, I'd just keep doing the job I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. A small itch at the back of my mind, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a decade's warning push you to plan a second career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. Tom would push me and I'd say I'll think about it at thirty-five. I know myself, I don't move till something's in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the paperwork side of your job when the thinking AI lands in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd be the first thing to go, the care plans and the notes. I'd be glad, it's the bit I'm slowest at. Then I'd have three years of just doing the hands-on part, which is the part I actually like.

say: I'd say it's a **long way off** and not worth losing sleep over.
I'd repeat my usual line that **people want people**.
think: Ten years feels like **someone else's problem**, which I know is a bit daft.
My job would be **safe through my thirties**, the part of life I'm planning.
do: Buy the **semi** we wanted and start trying for a **baby**.
Keep the **weekend shifts** and add a bit extra to my pension.
Skip **retraining** and keep doing the job I'm good at.
feel: **Settled**, with a small itch at the back of my mind.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like someone else's problem, and I know that's a bit daft.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **go ahead** with the house and children she already planned.
She admits she won't **plan a second career** until the change is in front of her.
She'd welcome AI taking the **care plans**, the part she's slowest at.

steps.text: Buy the semi-detached house we planned and try for a baby
Keep the weekend shifts and the same client round
Add a bit extra to the workplace pension each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there'd be no time to sort the house or anything else. What would help is the agency telling us straight what it's planning, and some kind of promise that people like me keep a job checking on clients. I don't want a course, I want to know where I stand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who'd want the robot. My clients wouldn't, but their kids living far away might, because it's cheaper and it never runs late. People who've never done a bed bath will be the ones deciding about care robots.

headlineQuote: People who've never done a bed bath will be the ones deciding about care robots.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old home carer** with seven years at the same agency and a known round of clients.
Weekend shifts, a partner's wage and **nine months saved** give her more security than most carers.
She avoids new technology and would **wait and watch** rather than move first.
The fast AGI picture makes her **pause the house**; a decade lets her carry on with family plans.
She'd want a **checking role** near her clients rather than retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to sort the house or anything else.
whatWouldHelp: The agency **telling staff straight** what it's planning.
A **promise** that carers like her keep jobs checking on clients.
